strengths: Well-motivated pivot from sample-level to token-level data selection, with clear identification of length and loss-centric biases in existing influence-based methods (Section 1)
Forward-only design is genuinely attractive for scalability; the asymptotic cost analysis (Section 5, Table 4) is careful and correctly distinguishes warmup vs. scoring costs across baselines

Evaluation covers several axes: in-domain budgeted accuracy (Table 1), low-overlap OOD math selection (Table 2), cross-model/cross-scale transfer with an oracle comparison (Table 3), length-bias analysis (Fig. 3), and task-adaptive source distribution analysis (Fig. 4)
Baselines are relevant and reasonably strong (LESS, TAGCOS, S2L, CLD, RDS, DSIR, BM25), with a shared warmup/selection pipeline to reduce confounds
Hyperparameter sensitivity is examined via a single-factor ablation study (Table 8), and the paper is honest in its limitations section about dependence on the small validation set
weaknesses: The core mechanism is heuristic and its central premise is not directly validated: no analysis shows that the attention-derived saliency actually identifies task-critical tokens or that fingerprints encode task structure; attention-as-importance is contested in the interpretability literature and the paper leans on prior work (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020) without evidence that this particular row/column heuristic is meaningful

Headline gains are modest on the main benchmark: Table 1 shows ~1.2 points over LESS (45.37 vs 44.21) with overlapping standard deviations, and the HELLASWAG improvement is within noise (49.08 vs 49.01); no statistical significance tests are reported, and the abstract's 'up to 9%' is driven by the single OOD GSM8K setting

The claimed orders-of-magnitude speedup is only supported by asymptotic analysis; the appendix explicitly states no wall-clock time or GPU-hours are reported (Appendix F.3), leaving the efficiency claim empirically unverified

Several design choices appear arbitrary and only ablated on one task/model (CSQA, Llama-3.2-1B): equal saliency weights, mean+max pooling, coverage term, penalty lambda, and number of layers; notably the ablation that 'None' penalty underperforms lambda=1.0 (Table 8) is confusing, since lambda=1.0 appears to be no penalty at all, and the distinction is not explained

Only LoRA fine-tuning and a limited task suite (3 multiple-choice benchmarks plus GSM8K) at 1B scale for the main results; generalization to full fine-tuning, larger scorer models, or generative evaluation is not shown

Fingerprints are built per token class from only 5-10 samples, meaning most classes will have very few occurrences and many candidates rely on the embedding-space backoff; the sensitivity of the method to this sparsity and to validation-set noise is not characterized (acknowledged but not analyzed)
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many pipeline details (scoring scope, coverage weight, backoff penalty) that affect results

strengths: Clear motivation and well-organized writing; the two-stage forward-only pipeline (attention-derived token saliency → class fingerprints → candidate scoring) is simple, easy to follow, and thoroughly described with pseudocode and hyperparameters.

Broad empirical evaluation: three multiple-choice tasks plus an out-of-domain GSM8K setting, cross-model/cross-scale transfer experiments (Llama-3.2-1B scorer → Llama-3.1-8B / Mistral-7B), length-distribution and source-distribution analyses, and an ablation table over the main hyperparameters.

The asymptotic cost analysis (Table 4) cleanly isolates where savings come from (single forward pass per candidate at one checkpoint, no backward passes at scoring time), and the framing of length bias and loss-centric bias in sample-level selection is a reasonable motivating angle.
Honest limitations section acknowledging sensitivity to the small target validation set and inapplicability to pretraining curation.
weaknesses: Headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. 'Outperform state-of-the-art baselines by up to 9%' is drawn exclusively from the GSM8K setting (29.52 vs. 20.72); on the main benchmarks (Table 1) the average gain over LESS is ~1.2 points (45.37 vs. 44.21) and 'surpassing full-data fine-tuning' margins (46.26 vs. 45.04 on SocialIQA; 49.08 vs. 48.55 on HellaSwag) are small and within roughly two standard deviations. The abstract and contributions present these as robust, general results.

The method is an accumulation of ad-hoc heuristics (attention entropy as row saliency, column-averaged attention, equal 0.5/0.5 weights, mean+max pooling, an OOV backoff, and a coverage bonus) with no theoretical or empirical validation of the core premise — e.g., no analysis showing that the derived saliency α_i actually identifies task-relevant tokens. Attention-as-importance is known to be unreliable, and the paper does not confront this.

Baseline fairness concerns: TRIM uses a task-specific scoring scope (prompt-only for CommonsenseQA, response-only for GSM8K) chosen per task, effectively giving it task-specific prior knowledge that baselines do not receive. Additionally, Eq. (13) in the main text omits the coverage term ηκ(c) that appears in Eq. (15) of the appendix, and Table 8 lists the default OOV 'penalty' as λ=1.0 (i.e., no penalty), contradicting the description of λ∈(0,1] as a down-weighting factor — the actual scoring procedure is unclear.

The central efficiency claim ('orders of magnitude faster') is never substantiated with wall-clock measurements; the authors explicitly decline to report GPU-hours and instead rely on asymptotic analysis, which is insufficient to support the claim as stated in the abstract.

The length-bias analysis (Section 4.4) does not support the conclusion that TRIM is 'length-agnostic': TRIM's score includes a coverage term that explicitly rewards longer token sets, and mean pooling over more tokens mechanically changes scores with length. The observed longer mean selection (446 tokens) may reflect this confound rather than genuine length-neutrality; no controlled experiment isolates the effect.

Transfer experiment (Table 3) compares TRIM-Transfer only against its own oracle and a random baseline; no gradient-based baseline (e.g., LESS) is transferred under the same protocol, so 'transfer with high fidelity' is not placed in comparative context. The GSM8K full-data baseline (30.25% for Llama-2-7B) is unusually low, making 'nearly matching full-data' easier than the framing implies.

The ablation study (Table 8) is limited to a single task (CommonsenseQA) and single model, and several ablations (e.g., last 6 vs. last 12 layers: 40.76 vs. 40.68) show the design is not particularly sensitive — raising the question of how much the specific saliency machinery matters versus the warmup plus token-level cosine matching. Related token-centric methods discussed in the related work (T-SHIRT, LADM) are not included as baselines.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, and reproduction of the full pipeline (warmup, LoRA configs, fingerprint construction) from the text alone would be difficult.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem (efficient, task-targeted coreset selection for instruction tuning) and the forward-only, token-level design is a genuinely different angle from the dominant gradient/loss-based sample-level paradigm.

The method is clearly specified: the saliency formulation (Eqs. 1-7), fingerprint construction, OOV backoff, and pooling are all described precisely, with pseudocode in Appendix B and shared hyperparameters in Appendix F, supporting reproducibility.

Experiments cover multiple axes: fixed-budget comparison against eight baselines (Table 1), low-overlap OOD math selection (Table 2), cross-model/cross-scale transfer (Table 3), length-bias analysis (Fig. 3), task-adaptive selection analysis (Figs. 4-5), an asymptotic cost comparison (Table 4), and hyperparameter ablations (Table 8). This is broader than many data-selection papers.
The cost analysis (Section 5) is a fair, like-for-like comparison that honestly accounts for warmup costs and checkpoint counts across baselines rather than only emphasizing TRIM's advantages.

The limitations section is honest about dependence on the small validation set and incompatibility with pretraining curation, and the treatment of the connection to linguistic collapse in Appendix A is unusually careful and appropriately hedged.
weaknesses: No wall-clock timing measurements are reported despite repeated claims that TRIM is 'orders of magnitude faster' (Abstract, contributions). The asymptotic analysis alone does not substantiate the constant factors; FLOP counts or measured GPU-hours for the full selection pipeline of TRIM vs. LESS/TAGCOS should be provided.

The headline 'up to 9%' improvement (Abstract, contributions) comes from a single task (GSM8K, ~8.8 points over LESS) in the OOD setting; on the main benchmark suite the margin over LESS is ~1.2 points on the macro average, which is only about 1-2 standard deviations given the reported seed variances. The abstract framing overstates the consistency of the gains.

The saliency heuristic is largely ad hoc: attention entropy as 'row saliency' and raw attention received as 'column saliency' inherit known pathologies of attention weights (e.g., positional/attention-sink artifacts, the fact that column sums are dominated by BOS-like tokens). The paper does not validate that the saliency scores actually correlate with token importance (e.g., against token-wise gradients on a small subset), which would directly test the central premise.

Diversity of the selected coreset is not addressed: TRIM is pure top-K scoring with no diversity or de-duplication mechanism, which is a core component of most coreset methods (e.g., TAGCOS, D2-Pruning). It apparently works anyway, but this deserves analysis or discussion.

There is no empirical comparison against the closest token-level baselines (T-SHIRT, LADM), which are discussed in the appendix but excluded from Tables 1-2 with only a cost argument. At least one token-centric baseline comparison would materially strengthen the 'token-level is better' claim.

There is an inconsistency between Eq. 13 in the main text (mean + max pooling) and Eq. 15 in the appendix (which adds a coverage term kappa with weight eta = 0.05); it is unclear which configuration produced the main results. Additionally, the ablation Table 8 labels lambda = 1.0 as the penalty default, which is effectively no penalty, making the 'None' vs '1.0' rows confusing.

Generalization is somewhat narrow: only LoRA fine-tuning, four target tasks, and models up to 8B; conclusions about scalability over 'massive instruction corpora' are not directly demonstrated beyond 270k examples.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly presented method: the two-stage forward-only pipeline (saliency-weighted token fingerprints + cosine-similarity candidate scoring) is easy to follow, well-illustrated in Figure 1, and fully specified with pseudocode (Appendix B) and implementation details (Appendix C).

Strong efficiency contribution: the asymptotic cost analysis in Section 5 is grounded in measured wall-clock runtimes (Table 5), showing TRIM at 4.4 hours vs. 14–88 hours for gradient/trajectory baselines — a genuine and practical advantage that is convincingly analyzed.

Comprehensive and unusually thorough evaluation: main benchmarks (Table 1), budget sweeps (Figure 2), a challenging low-overlap setting (GSM8K from a non-math pool, Table 2), cross-model/scale transfer (Tables 3, 24), length-bias analysis (Figure 3), an in-domain no-target regime (Section 4.5, Appendix M), and extensive ablations (layers, pooling, IDF, NFF penalty, checkpoints, target-set size, noisy targets) in Appendices H–N.

The GSM8K low-overlap result (29.52% vs. LESS 20.72% at 5%) is a striking demonstration that token-level structural matching can recover reasoning-style data that sample-level signals miss, and the source-composition analysis (Figure 4) and qualitative fingerprints (Table 17) make the mechanism interpretable.

Robustness analyses (target-set size, noisy targets in Appendix J) and out-of-task evaluation (Appendix I) address obvious concerns about fragility of attention-derived saliency; the impact statement thoughtfully discusses bias-amplification risks of data curation.
weaknesses: Headline gains on the main general-domain benchmarks are marginal and arguably within noise: TRIM's mean of 48.56 vs. LESS's 48.27 on Table 1 (MMLU 49.33 vs. 49.23; BBH std 0.89) is not a clear statistical improvement. The 'outperforms state-of-the-art by up to 9%' claim in the abstract rests essentially on the single GSM8K setting, and the abstract/intro framing overstates the generality of this result.

Novelty is moderate: the ingredients (attention-entropy saliency, column-attention 'hub' scores, IDF reweighting, cosine-similarity to prototypes, mean/max pooling) are each well-established, and the paper itself acknowledges grounding in attention-flow, copy-mechanism, and token-sparsification prior work (Appendix A). The contribution is a sensible engineering combination rather than a new principle, and the connection to token-level influence (Lin et al., 2024a) is asserted but not empirically validated (e.g., no comparison against token-wise gradient influence even at small scale).

In the in-domain no-target regime (Tables 4 and 20), TRIM does not outperform S2L or LESS (e.g., MATHINSTRUCT averages 52.00 vs. 52.16 for S2L); the contribution there reduces to 'comparable accuracy at lower cost,' which weakens the breadth of claimed superiority.

Some design choices appear brittle or under-justified: the pooling ablation (Table 10) shows sharp sensitivity to the coverage weight (49.43 at 0.05 vs. 48.77 at 0.10), and minor inconsistencies exist between reported default numbers (Table 1: 49.33 vs. ablation default 49.43) without explanation. The length-bias mitigation claim is supported only descriptively via selected-length distributions, not by a causal analysis.

No explicit statement of code release is provided; given the many hyperparameters (wQ/wK, λ, pooling weights, L, scoring scope, coverage η), reproducibility would depend heavily on released code, which is not indicated.

Reliance on a warmup phase on 5% of the pool is inherited from LESS, but its interaction with the attention-saliency mechanism is not analyzed; Table 13 shows large dependence on the warmup checkpoint (44.26 pretrained vs. 49.43 warmed), so selection quality is sensitive to a component the method does not control.

strengths: The core idea is appealing and practical: replacing per-sample gradient computation with a forward-only, token-level fingerprint matching scheme is a sensible efficiency contribution, and the paper is well positioned relative to gradient-based (LESS, TAGCOS), training-dynamics (S2L, CLD), and heuristic (BM25, DSIR) baselines.

The computational cost analysis (Section 5, Table 5) is a genuine strength: it provides both asymptotic analysis and measured wall-clock runtimes under a shared setup, clearly delineating warmup vs. scoring costs. TRIM's 4.4h vs. LESS's 35.8h is a real, demonstrated efficiency gain.

The experimental scope is broad: multiple budgets (Fig. 2), cross-model/scale transfer (Table 3), a low-overlap GSM8K setting (Table 2), a target-free in-domain setting (Section 4.5), sensitivity-to-target-size and noise robustness ablations (Appendix J), and a supplementary model family (Appendix N).

Detailed appendices (pseudocode, hyperparameters, baseline descriptions, dataset provenance, licenses) support reproducibility, and the impact statement thoughtfully addresses bias-amplification risks of targeted data curation.

The GSM8K low-overlap result (29.52% vs. 20.72% for LESS at 5%, nearly matching full-data fine-tuning) is a striking finding, and the length-distribution analysis (Fig. 3) offers a plausible, checkable account of why token-level scoring behaves differently from sample-level scoring.
weaknesses: Overclaimed headline results. The abstract claims TRIM 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 9%,' but on the main benchmark suite (Table 1) the margin over LESS is 0.29% (48.56 vs. 48.27), with overlapping standard deviations (BBH: 39.73±0.89 vs. 39.45±0.2; MMLU: 49.33±0.4 vs. 49.23±0.3). No statistical significance tests are reported anywhere. The 9% figure rests entirely on the single GSM8K setting, and 'consistently outperform' is not supported by Table 1.

The 'orders of magnitude faster' claim (Introduction) is contradicted by the paper's own Table 5: TRIM's total selection runtime (4.40h) is ~3.2x faster than TAGCOS (14.16h) and ~8x faster than LESS (35.76h) — meaningful, but not orders of magnitude, and the intro's efficiency framing also obscures that TRIM still requires the same LoRA warmup fine-tuning as LESS.

Internal inconsistencies between the main text and appendix default configuration. Eq. (13) in the main paper defines the sample score as 0.5·mean + 0.5·max, but Appendix C/H reveal the actual default includes a +0.05·coverage term. Moreover, the ablation tables report inconsistent MMLU values for the 'default' configuration (49.43 in Tables 10–13 vs. 49.33 in Table 1 and Table 9). These discrepancies undermine confidence in which configuration produced the headline numbers.

Hyperparameters appear tuned on the evaluation benchmark. All ablations (number of layers, pooling function, IDF, NFF penalty λ, checkpoints) are conducted on MMLU — one of the four benchmarks reported in the main results — and the 'default' configuration is highlighted based on those results. This creates a test-task selection concern for the main table.

The method is a stack of heuristics (attention entropy row saliency, column attention, min-max rescaling, IDF reweighting, NFF fallback with penalty λ, mean/max/coverage pooling) whose individual contributions are small and task-dependent (e.g., IDF slightly hurts on MMLU: 49.31 vs. 49.43). There is no direct validation that the attention-derived saliency signal itself correlates with token importance — a known weakness of attention-as-explanation — so the mechanism behind the gains remains speculative.

The most related token-centric baselines are discussed but not empirically compared. T-SHIRT, LADM, and QCS are characterized in Related Work and Appendix A, yet Table 1 contains no token-level competitors; the comparison set is dominated by sample-level methods, weakening the claim that token-level resolution is the decisive factor rather than simply the specific heuristic used.

Key positive results are under-analyzed. The near-full-data GSM8K result (29.52 vs. 30.25) is a large, surprising gap over LESS (20.72), but the explanation ('structural fidelity', 'transferable proxies for chain-of-thought structure') is qualitative; there is a single deterministic selection per method, so variance from selection itself (vs. fine-tuning seeds) is unquantified. The length-bias analysis (Fig. 3) is descriptive only, with no causal link established between longer selected samples and downstream gains.

Marginal-value components and scope: in the in-domain setting (Table 4), TRIM is essentially tied with S2L/LESS (within noise), so the method's advantage is concentrated in targeted-selection settings; the paper's broad framing ('scalable and efficient alternative for building high-quality instruction-tuning datasets') extends beyond what is demonstrated. No explicit code release statement is provided.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: shifting from sample-level influence signals to token-level, attention-derived saliency fingerprints, which directly addresses documented failure modes (length bias, loss-centric credit assignment) of existing coreset selection methods.

The method is genuinely efficient: a careful cost analysis (Section 5) with both asymptotic complexity and measured wall-clock runtimes on shared hardware supports the claim that TRIM is substantially cheaper than gradient-based alternatives (4.40h vs. 14.16–87.95h for baselines).

The experimental coverage is broad and fairly thorough: multiple baselines grouped by mechanism, budget sweeps (Figure 2), a challenging low-overlap GSM8K setting (Table 2), cross-model/cross-architecture transfer (Tables 3 and 24), a no-target in-domain regime (Section 4.5, Appendix M), and extensive hyperparameter ablations (Appendices H–J) including sensitivity to target-set size and noisy targets.

The qualitative analyses add credibility: token-level fingerprints (Table 17), NFF fallback examples (Table 18), source-composition analysis (Figure 4), and length-distribution evidence for the length-bias claim (Figure 3).
Reproducibility is aided by detailed appendices (pseudocode, hyperparameters, dataset construction, licenses) and an honest impact statement discussing selection-induced bias amplification.
weaknesses: The headline 'up to 9% improvement' is driven almost entirely by the 1%-budget GSM8K setting (Table 2); on the main benchmark suite (Table 1), the improvement over LESS is only +0.29 average points, which is within or comparable to the reported standard deviations (e.g., BBH std 0.89 vs. gap 0.28). Statistical significance is not assessed, so the claim of 'consistently outperforming state-of-the-art' is stronger than the evidence.

The mechanism relies on attention weights as importance signals, a known-to-be-fragile practice; the paper provides correlation-style evidence (length distributions, source compositions) but no direct validation that the attention-derived saliency identifies tokens that actually cause task gains (e.g., token-level intervention or leave-one-out checks).

Several design choices appear heuristic and post-hoc: the mean+max pooling with a small coverage bonus (Table 10 shows the specific 0.05 weight performs best while neighbors are worse), the NFF penalty λ=0.9 (Table 12 shows large sensitivity, 44.79→49.43), and last-6-layer aggregation. Ablations are only reported on MMLU; it is unclear whether the same settings transfer across tasks, raising overfitting-to-benchmark concerns.

It is not established that the gains come from 'attention-derived' structure rather than simply token-level IDF-weighted embedding similarity; a cheap baseline using embedding/lexical token matching without attention saliency would isolate the contribution of the saliency machinery, and the IDF ablation (Table 11) shows it barely matters.

The transfer experiments (Table 3) contain internal tension: TRIM-Transfer exceeds the in-model oracle on several cells (e.g., TyDiQA 56.70 vs. 54.12 on 13B), which is only loosely explained and suggests seed noise or confounds in the protocol.
No code release or artifact statement is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a method with many implementation details (NFF caching, selective scoring scopes, coverage term).
